source.title: OWLS: Scaling Laws for Multilingual Speech Recognition and Translation Models
source.authors: William Chen; Jin-Chuan Tian; Yifan Peng; Brian Yan; Chao-Han Huck Yang; Shinji Watanabe

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through the appendix. Some figure-axis text is garbled, but the surrounding prose and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law investigations to multilingual speech recognition and speech translation. It evaluates WER, CER and BLEU scaling, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports ASR/ST scaling results and downstream task outcomes. It does not measure language-model pretraining cross-entropy or test a fixed-compute parameter/token allocation. Results from unrelated comparisons and emergent-ability experiments are not cataloged as scaling-law results.
record.test_reason: The study trains 0.25B–18B multilingual speech encoder-decoder models and fits power laws of WER/CER and BLEU against parameters and compute. It also varies training data (11K–360K h). This is a new modality and measure for the scaling claim (V5). The zero-shot code-switching results bear on downstream predictability (V6). It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is mostly right. The authors conclude that scaling parameters, data and compute gives reasonable direct predictions of downstream ASR/ST performance, and that model scaling helps low-resource languages. They identify failure cases: too little task data, and same-distribution data that quickly saturates without added diversity. They also claim that emergent abilities (in-context learning, orthographic understanding, code-switching, mondegreens) appear in larger speech models.
record.recipe_differences: This is a supervised multilingual speech encoder-decoder study. It evaluates WER, CER and BLEU on ASR/ST tasks rather than measuring held-out text pretraining cross-entropy or fitting the original language-model loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary by language, task, data distribution and available task-specific data. The paper reports that adding data from a new distribution helps some languages after same-distribution scaling has saturated, while more same-distribution data can cause language-specific degradations.
record.problems: The study measures downstream speech-task error and translation scores rather than held-out pretraining loss. Some outcomes are available only as figures, and some scaling evaluations are limited to selected languages. The text reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional per-language and per-model figure/table values, plus further ASR/ST benchmark comparisons. These were not extracted where the text provided no separately stated numeric outcome relevant to the selected scaling-law versions; the relevant scaling-curve summaries and named exceptions are recorded above.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy is reported. Only WER/CER/BLEU are reported.
No fit on small models is used to predict much larger runs. r13 predicts a run's final WER from its own early checkpoints, not across scale.
There is no fixed-compute sweep over the parameter/data split.
Depth and width change together with size (Table 7). Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Cross-entropy loss form, irreducible-loss term, image/video, repeated data and fine-tuning/transfer are not tested. Only speech ASR/ST error metrics are covered.
Downstream performance is not related to pretraining loss. Only zero-shot code-switching and emergent-ability evaluations are downstream.
No comparison of fitting choices or published exponents.

missing.what: There is no row for the per-language ASR data-quantity correlation with WER/CER. It is only R2≃0.5, and the authors say no language-agnostic data law can be fit.

There is no row for scaling from 9B to 18B. Gains bend or reverse for several languages, e.g. Portuguese WER 14.1→21.1, Czech 29.5→36.1, Swedish improves only 40.7→39.1. LibriSpeech is 1.9→2.0, and Japanese Reazon is 7.3→7.5.

There are no rows for the emergent and zero-shot downstream evaluations. In mondegreen tests, PPL is 372 at 9B vs 429 at 18B, and MOS is 4.8 vs 4.4. In Quechua ICL, 9B is best (27.4 CER, k=3). In contextual biasing, 0.25B collapses to ~97% WER and only 9B lowers overall WER.
There is no row for the test-time compute-matched comparison. At about 40–50 TFLOPS, WER is 4.52 for 9B vs 8.33 for 0.25B.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows were relinked from V6 to V5. The OWLS models are supervised speech-to-text models evaluated on their own training tasks, so WER/BLEU here is the in-task held-out metric, not downstream LM performance. The power law is fitted to WER with no irreducible term, and fit quality is reported only as R2. The paper gives no exponents or uncertainty. Data scaling is tested only at 1B. Its 360K point mixes in a new distribution, and ST results exclude 360K.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss.
It predicts downstream WER from model-size or compute curves, not held-out cross-entropy loss of much larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimizing parameter/token split is tested.
Depth and width are scaled together; their separate effects at fixed parameter count are not tested.

The tested modality is multilingual speech, with downstream WER/CER/BLEU measures rather than pretraining cross-entropy. The study does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
The study tests downstream ASR and ST metrics against model size, training data and compute, not downstream performance against pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitting choices or published exponents, or test whether curves bend away from a power law because of fitting setup.

conditions.value: AMI, LibriSpeech, SPGISpeech, Tedlium, VoxPopuli, GigaSpeech

rows.note: The paper reports the average across the six benchmarks and says ASR improves across all domains.
rows.check: This is in-task held-out ASR WER of a supervised speech model, so it is not 'downstream' of LM pretraining. Relinked from V6 to V5.

rows.subject: OWLS model-size sweep
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated FLEURS WER/CER across model sizes and fitted language-specific model-size scaling curves.
rows.measure: Coefficient of determination, R2, for language-specific model-size scaling laws predicting WER/CER
rows.note: This is a reported aggregate characterization of language-specific fits, not a per-language value.
rows.check: The R2 is a fit-quality summary of a WER=βN^α power law with no irreducible term, not a loss law. V6 link dropped, since this is the training-task metric.

relationships.condition: Model-size and training-compute scaling of speech ASR/ST (0.25B–9B)
relationships.reason: WER/CER follow language-specific power laws in N (R2≃0.95). WER, low-resource WER and BLEU improve with size, and final WER tracks compute (R2≃0.82) (r1–r5, r13).
relationships.display_finding: WER and CER followed model-size power laws with R² approximately 0.95, final WER tracked compute with R² approximately 0.82, and recognition and translation metrics improved with size.

relationships.condition: Data-size scaling at fixed 1B parameters, and tasks with negligible task data
relationships.reason: Same-distribution data scaling saturates or degrades for some languages. ST data correlates only loosely with BLEU (R2≃0.55), and en→de BLEU falls with more data (r7, r11, r12). Gains need new-distribution data (r8–r10). Japanese ST does not improve with size (r6).
relationships.display_finding: Same-distribution gains saturated or reversed, speech-translation data explained BLEU only loosely with R² ≈ 0.55, English-to-German BLEU declined with more data, and Japanese speech translation showed no model-size gain.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot code-switched ASR, Latin-script languages (e.g. Portuguese)
relationships.reason: Code-switched CER falls significantly with model size (r15).
relationships.display_finding: Code-switched character error decreased significantly with model size.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot code-switched ASR, languages with very different orthography (e.g. Chinese)
relationships.reason: The authors state that Chinese code-switching sees no improvement with scale (r14).
relationships.display_finding: Chinese code-switching performance showed no improvement as model scale increased.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
